Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) read company news at scale, and backtests suggest that their readings predict stock returns. We ask how much of that predictability survives a test that rules out look-ahead, memorization and selection. We propose OLIVIA, a protocol for such tests: point-in-time inputs with company identities masked, selection on validation data only, an analysis plan frozen by cryptographic hash, and a test period unblinded once through a logged lock. We apply it to AI decision models, non-generative language models that return probabilities for typed questions, reading news about S&P 500 stocks: an open-weights model we fine-tuned on 2024–2025 data, three commercial models and standard baselines. The fine-tuned model’s signal replicated on two validation quarters (daily information coefficients 0.055 and 0.065) but fell to 0.020 (t=1.7t=1.7) on the blinded January–July 2026 test. The commercial models’ readings line up with the overnight move to the open (information coefficient 0.074 to 0.077) but not with the move after it, so the news is priced by the time a trader can act on it at the open. No model can tell over- from under-reaction, and no pre-registered strategy survives costs and a deflated Sharpe ratio. Commercial models identify masked companies in 62% to 74% of cases against a 28% baseline: masking hides names, not companies. The market reads the news first.

Keywords: large language models (LLMs); financial news; stock return prediction; look-ahead bias; memorization; pre-registration; overnight returns; market efficiency.

JEL codes: G14, G12, C45, C52, C12.

1 Introduction

Much company news is published before the stock market opens. Two questions follow. Can a model that reads that news anticipate how the price will react? And once part of the reaction is visible, can it tell whether the market moved too far or not far enough? Both are old questions in empirical finance. Prices react to firm news within minutes (Patell and Wolfson, 1984; Busse and Green, 2002), media tone predicts short-horizon returns (Tetlock, 2007), and moves that come with news tend to drift while moves without news tend to reverse (Chan, 2003). Large language models (LLMs) now read news at scale, and several studies find that their readings predict returns (Lopez-Lira and Tang, 2026; Chen et al., 2022). We ask whether such predictability survives a test built to rule out the usual ways a backtest misleads: look-ahead in the data, memorization in the model and selection over many variants.

We study AI decision models. A decision model is a non-generative model that takes a state (text plus structured context) and a set of typed questions (a choice among options, a score on an ordered scale, or a yes-or-no question) and returns probabilities over the answers instead of generating text (Zhu et al., 2026). Decision models are close relatives of LLM-based classifiers and of probabilistic forecasting with language models (Kadavath et al., 2022; Halawi et al., 2024; Schoenegger et al., 2024), and their vendors describe the probabilities as calibrated. They suit finance because they return the quantities a forecaster needs, such as a distribution over the size of the coming move, at a cost of a few cents per thousand decisions, and because open-weights versions can be fine-tuned.

Language models also bring a specific threat. A model trained on text published after the period on which it is tested may know how events turned out, and even a model with an earlier training cutoff can recognize a company from the content of its news (Glasserman and Lin, 2024; Sarkar and Vafa, 2024; Lopez-Lira et al., 2025). A backtest of a language-model signal on historical news therefore mixes the model’s ability to read news with its memory of what followed. A second threat is older: when many signals, filters and horizons are tried, the best backtest overstates what a strategy will earn (Harvey et al., 2016; Bailey and López de Prado, 2014). Pre-registration, fixing the analysis before the data are seen, is the standard remedy in other sciences and is still rare in empirical finance (Harvey, 2017; Olken, 2015).

We combine these elements in OLIVIA, a protocol for testing language-model signals on financial news without look-ahead (Table ), and apply it to the point-in-time S&P 500 from July 2024 to July 2026 (Figure ). For each company and trading session we build the news state as of 09:15 ET and mask company names, tickers, people, dates and every mention of a price move. Before the open, each model gives a pre-open reading: how the stock will perform once the news is absorbed. At 10:00 and after the close it gives a post-reaction reading: was the reaction so far too small or too large for the news? The primary instrument, Laya-Fin, is an open-weights decision model that we fine-tuned on 2024–2025 news and returns; we compare it with three commercial decision models, the untuned Laya model and standard baselines. The hypotheses and selection rules were written down before any data were analyzed, and every later change is dated in an append-only log; selection used two validation quarters of 2025, and the analysis plan was frozen by hash before the 2026 test outcomes were unblinded, once.

Key findings.

  1. (1)

    Pre-open news is priced at the open. The commercial models’ readings line up with the overnight move from the previous close to the open (daily information coefficient, IC, 0.074 to 0.077) but not with the move after the open (about zero). No model predicts the move after the open, which is the part a trader who reads the news before the open can still earn. The untuned Laya model, which barely recognizes masked companies, shows the same split.

  2. (2)

    A validated signal did not survive the blinded test. Laya-Fin’s IC with the day’s move was 0.065 (t=3.6t=3.6) in the final validation quarter and 0.020 (t=1.7t=1.7) on the test. Every model whose validation IC was clearly positive fell, none of the five primary hypotheses is supported, and no pre-registered strategy survives costs and a deflated Sharpe ratio. In exploratory analyses, the signal that remained sat on earnings days, and conditions selected on two validation quarters, with in-sample Sharpe ratios up to 6.8, failed on the test.

  3. (3)

    The models cannot judge the reaction. In the pre-registered over/under regression the news coefficient is not positive (Laya-Fin b=−0.044b=-0.044, p=0.62p=0.62), and the moves the models call underreactions never catch up. Out of sample, same-day news explains 0.25% (Laya-Fin) to 0.82% (d1-ultra) of a stock’s own daily variance, and the commercial models’ stated probabilities overstate their accuracy.

  4. (4)

    Masking is not anonymity. Given masked news, the commercial models pick the company out of four same-sector candidates in 62% to 74% of cases, against a matched baseline of 28%; the open-weights Laya model does so in 32%.

Contributions.

First, we give OLIVIA, a protocol of six safeguards (one-time unblinding, look-ahead-free states, identity masking, validation-only selection, an immutable plan and an audit trail), which Table  lists as a checklist that other studies can adopt. Second, we give a test of whether a language-model news signal can be traded: splitting each day’s move at the open shows that the predictable part of pre-open news is already in the opening price. Third, we add two measurement tools for language models in finance: a matched-distractor test of whether a model recognizes masked companies, and a firm-level version of the explanation ladder of Kelly et al. (2026), which measures how much of a stock’s own daily move its news explains.

Section  reviews related work and Section  describes the data and the design. Sections  to  report the pre-registered results, nulls included. Section  reports exploratory analyses, labeled post hoc, and Section  the limitations and a pre-registered forward test on news published after the models’ release.

2 Related work

Language models and stock returns.

Text has long been used to predict returns, from dictionary measures of the tone of news (Tetlock, 2007; Tetlock et al., 2008) to sentiment scores learned from returns (Ke et al., 2019). Large language models extend this line. Lopez-Lira and Tang (2026) find that ChatGPT’s reading of headlines predicts the returns that follow. For news released overnight, it predicts the move from the previous close to the open, which they note only an insider or a trader with early access could exploit, and a smaller drift from the open to the close, which they trade and which turns unprofitable at 20 basis points per round trip; our hypothesis H1b tests that open-to-close leg. Chen et al. (2022) find that LLM representations of news predict the cross-section of returns. Kelly et al. (2026) use generative AI to explain realized market returns with the reasons given in daily market summaries, revisiting Roll (1988), who found that market, industry and public news explain only a small part of individual stock returns; we carry their explanation ladder to the firm level. Decision models are a newer interface (Zhu et al., 2026): the model returns probabilities for typed questions instead of text, so no free text needs parsing and every output is a forecast that can be scored.

Look-ahead bias and memorization.

Glasserman and Lin (2024) test for look-ahead bias in GPT’s sentiment readings of news by anonymizing the companies; Sarkar and Vafa (2024) analyze look-ahead bias in pretrained language models used for prediction; Lopez-Lira et al. (2025) show that LLMs recall economic and financial data from their training period, so forecasting tests inside that period are not out of sample; He et al. (2026) train language models only on text available at each date; and Ludwig et al. (2026) argue that a language model can be used for prediction only if its training data exclude the evaluation sample, which undisclosed training data rarely allow a researcher to verify. In machine learning, memorization and benchmark contamination are documented and measured directly (Carlini et al., 2023; Golchin and Surdeanu, 2024; Sainz et al., 2023). Every decision model we use was released after our sample ended, so none can be assumed ignorant of it. We therefore mask the states, measure how often a model still identifies the company, and pre-register a forward test on news published after the models’ release.

News, attention and price reactions.

Prices incorporate firm news quickly (Patell and Wolfson, 1984; Busse and Green, 2002) but not always completely. Earnings news drifts (Bernard and Thomas, 1989); price moves that come with news continue while moves without identifiable news reverse (Chan, 2003; Savor, 2012); high-frequency evidence points to underreaction to news (Jiang et al., 2021); and identifying the relevant news sharpens the link between information and volatility (Boudoukh et al., 2019). Stale or recombined news is mispriced (Tetlock, 2011; Fedyk and Hodson, 2023), and distracted or inattentive investors underreact (Hirshleifer et al., 2009; DellaVigna and Pollet, 2009). Behavioral models explain both underreaction and overreaction (Barberis et al., 1998; Daniel et al., 1998), building on the overreaction evidence of De Bondt and Thaler (1985), while Fama (1998) argues that the two kinds of anomaly are about equally frequent and fragile to the choice of method. The split of a daily return into an overnight and an intraday part (Lou et al., 2019) is central here: we ask on which side of the open the news is priced. Much of the price discovery for news released outside regular hours happens in after-hours and pre-market trading (Barclay and Hendershott, 2003), and the overnight returns of stocks that attract attention partly reverse during the trading day (Berkman et al., 2012).

Selective prediction and calibration.

A model that can abstain trades coverage for accuracy (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017), and whether its confidence is a useful guide depends on calibration, which modern neural networks often lack (Pakdaman Naeini et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2017). Language models are partly calibrated about what they know (Kadavath et al., 2022), and LLM forecasts can approach the accuracy of human forecasters (Halawi et al., 2024; Schoenegger et al., 2024). We measure calibration with the pre-registered expected calibration error and use selective prediction only in the exploratory section.

Pre-registration and replication in finance.

Many published return predictors do not survive multiple-testing adjustments or replication (Harvey et al., 2016; Hou et al., 2020), although Jensen et al. (2023) find that most factors replicate once the evidence is aggregated properly, and the returns to published predictors fall out of sample and after publication (McLean and Pontiff, 2016). Harvey (2017) calls for pre-registration and other safeguards in financial economics, and Olken (2015) discusses the benefits and limits of pre-analysis plans in economics. For trading strategies, the deflated Sharpe ratio adjusts a backtest for the number of trials behind it (Bailey and López de Prado, 2014). We pre-register hypotheses, families and corrections, log every trial, and report every pre-registered result.

Our earlier work.

Kargarzadeh et al. (2026) ask when news is priced in, using millions of news articles on about three thousand US stocks, each tagged by an LLM-distilled classifier with an event type and several attributes. They find that the reaction is concentrated before and on the day of publication, that markets underreact to numbers and overreact to stories, and that news carries width as well as direction. This paper extends that work in three ways. It replaces the event tags with decision models that read the masked news and forecast the move directly; it splits the reaction at the open and at fixed decision points, so that it can ask whether a reader of the news can trade on it; and it moves from a descriptive study to a pre-registered, blinded test with a single unblinding.

3 Data and design

The design implements the OLIVIA protocol (Table ); Figure  sets out its calendar and one trading session. The pre-registration, its amendments and its deviations log are part of the replication package. Appendix  summarizes the material deviations, and Appendix Table A1 collects the notation.

3.1 Universe, sample periods and returns

The universe is the point-in-time membership of the S&P 500: a stock is in the sample on a session only if it was an index member on that session, and companies with several share classes count once. Each month the members are split into three size tiers by market capitalization at the previous month-end: the 100 largest, ranks 101–250 and ranks 251–500. The sample is split by time into a training period (2024-07-01 to 2025-06-30), two validation quarters and a test period. The first validation quarter, val-A (2025-07-01 to 2025-09-30), is used for search and for fitting calibration maps, temperatures and thresholds; the second, val-B (2025-10-01 to 2025-12-31), for confirmation and the final selection. The test period, 2026-01-02 to 2026-07-31, was blinded until the analysis plan was frozen and was then unblinded once. A target enters an evaluation only if its whole horizon ends inside its period, and the first five sessions of each evaluation period are left out.

Daily prices are adjusted for splits, dividends and spin-offs, and the opening price is put on the same basis. For stock ii on session tt, the close-to-close return splits at the open into an overnight return, from the previous close to the open, and an intraday return, from the open to the close:

1+ri,tc​c=(1+ri,to​n)​(1+ri,ti​d),zi,tk=ARi,tkσi,t−1k,k∈{c​c,o​n,i​d}.1+r^{cc}_{i,t}=\bigl(1+r^{on}_{i,t}\bigr)\bigl(1+r^{id}_{i,t}\bigr),\qquad z^{k}_{i,t}=\frac{\mathrm{AR}^{k}_{i,t}}{\sigma^{k}_{i,t-1}},\quad k\in\{cc,on,id\}. (1)

In logs, the close-to-close move is the sum of the overnight move and the move after the open. Each part is made abnormal by removing the market and the stock’s sector, ARi,tk=ri,tk−βim​rm,tk−βis​(rs,tk−rm,tk)\mathrm{AR}^{k}_{i,t}=r^{k}_{i,t}-\beta^{m}_{i}\,r^{k}_{m,t}-\beta^{s}_{i}\,(r^{k}_{s,t}-r^{k}_{m,t}), where rmr_{m} is the return of the S&P 500 ETF (SPY), rsr_{s} the equal-weighted return of the other members of the stock’s sector, and the betas come from the 252 sessions up to t−1t-1. It is then divided by σi,t−1k\sigma^{k}_{i,t-1}, a robust scale of the stock’s abnormal returns over the 126 sessions up to t−1t-1. A value of zi,tkz^{k}_{i,t} is therefore a move in units of the stock’s typical daily move, scaled by information known before the session. Equation () defines what “priced at the open” means in this paper: news is priced at the open when a model’s reading predicts zo​nz^{on} but not zi​dz^{id}. Where the indices are clear we write zc​cz_{cc}, zo​nz_{on} and zi​dz_{id}, as the tables and figures do. Multi-day targets add up abnormal returns over their window and divide by the window’s ex-ante volatility; the main one, y2y_{2}, runs from the next open to the close of t+5t+5.

3.2 News, events and decision points

The news comes from NewsWitch, a commercial company-news feed (titles and snippets with publication times). An article is available at its time stamp, or at the end of the hour or day when the stamp is rounded to the hour or carries only a date. We drop items marked as non-news, price commentary and promotion, automatic institutional-holdings reports, non-English articles, near-duplicates, and two kinds of item whose time stamp precedes its content: explainers of a stock’s move and running market stories updated in place. We fix three decision points per session tt:

  • •

    D0, at 09:15 ET, before the open. The model reads the news published since the previous close; a trade enters at the official open.

  • •

    D1, at 10:00 ET, after the first 30-minute bar. The model also sees the move so far; a trade enters at the price at the end of that bar.

  • •

    D2, after the close. The model reads the day’s news and the day’s move; a trade enters at the next open.

The observed reaction GG is the move up to the decision point in typical-move units: at D2 it is the day’s zc​cz_{cc}, and at D1 the abnormal move from the previous close to 10:00, divided by its ex-ante volatility.

A learned importance filter, a logistic regression on sentence embeddings of the news (Xiao et al., 2024), selects the company-days that enter the analysis. Chosen on val-A by a pre-registered rule, it captures 43.5% of the company-days with a material price reaction at a budget of 30% of covered company-days. An event is a company-session with selected news: D0 events use the news up to 09:15, D2 events the news up to the close. The test period has 13,748 D0 events on 140 sessions and 17,188 D2 events.

Each event becomes a state, a JSON document with fixed keys: the company’s context (sector, size tier, market sensitivity, volatility regime, recent abnormal performance, analyst-estimate revisions and whether an earnings report is scheduled), the market’s context (the previous session’s market move, the level and change of the VIX, rates, credit spreads, the dollar, oil and scheduled macroeconomic releases), attention (the number of articles against the stock’s usual number) and up to six news items with their source type and timing. Every number passes through a codebook of words: a move of between one and two typical daily moves is “moderate”, followed by its multiple of a typical day’s move. A post-reaction state adds the reaction so far: the stock’s move, the market’s move over the same period and the volume against normal.

The two readings.

The pre-open reading asks, among other questions, “Once investors fully absorb the news, how will the company’s stock perform relative to the overall market and its sector over the next five trading days?” on nine levels, from a very large fall (more than three typical daily moves) to a very large rise. With pkp_{k} the probability of level kk and mkm_{k} the level’s midpoint in typical daily moves, the news-implied move is the model’s expected move,

N^=∑k=19pk​mk,m=(−3.5,−2.5,−1.5,−0.75, 0, 0.75, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5).\hat{N}=\sum_{k=1}^{9}p_{k}m_{k},\qquad m=(-3.5,\ -2.5,\ -1.5,\ -0.75,\ 0,\ 0.75,\ 1.5,\ 2.5,\ 3.5).

The news-implied value VV maps N^\hat{N} to the realized five-day level move with an isotonic regression (Barlow et al., 1972) fitted on val-A for each model: it is the model’s estimate of where the abnormal price settles once the news is absorbed. The post-reaction reading also asks whether the reaction so far is in the wrong direction, much too small, too small, about right, too large or much too large for what the news justifies, and whether the move will reverse, stall or continue over the next five days. Its judgment J=P⁡(much too small)+P⁡(too small)−P⁡(too large)−P⁡(much too large)J=P(\text{much too small})+P(\text{too small})-P(\text{too large})-P(\text{much too large}) is positive when the model calls the reaction an underreaction. A pre-registered check found that the post-reaction readings anchor on the move the model is shown, so N^\hat{N} always comes from the pre-open reading.

Masking.

The states hide the company. Names, aliases, tickers and cashtags become “the company”; person names become “an executive” or “a person”; dates, weekdays, years and fiscal-period labels become “recently” or “the latest quarter”; share-price levels and every percent price move of any security (the company’s, other companies’, indexes, commodities and currencies) are removed. Fundamental figures, such as earnings per share, revenue and guidance, are kept, because they are the news. An independent leak scanner, written without the masker’s rules, checked the result; the residues that remain, below half a percent of states for names, tickers and dates, are disclosed in the deviations log. Masking cannot hide a company whose news is distinctive, and Section  measures how often the models still recognize it.

3.3 The models

Laya-Fin, the primary instrument.

Laya is an open-weights decision model built on the ModernBERT-large encoder (Convai Innovations, 2026; Warner et al., 2025). We fine-tuned it on the training period’s states with three heads: the nine-level move (labeled with the realized five-day move), a five-level magnitude head (the size of the same-day move) and, for the post-reaction reading, a three-class continuation head. It was trained once (one seed, one epoch) with AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) and early stopping on val-A, and one temperature per head was fitted on val-A; the pre-registered second and third seeds are robustness runs (Section ).

Commercial decision models.

Every eligible decision model in a public model router’s catalog, plus the local Laya models, entered a two-stage zero-shot tournament on val-A. The six with the highest first-stage IC then faced four pre-registered screens: company identification on masked states, the share of counterfactual edits (beat or miss, raise or cut, upgrade or downgrade) that move the reading the right way, the IC gain from unmasking, and a shuffled-news control. No model passed: all six recognized the masked company far more often than the screen allowed (Section ), and five also failed the counterfactual screen. By a decision logged before the freeze, the three with the highest second-stage IC, d1-ultra, span-02 and drex-v2.0, were carried to the test as screen-failing comparators (the API models of the tables and figures). We refer to them by short labels because the results concern the versions we tested; the replication package lists their catalog identifiers and release dates. All three were released in October 2026, after the sample ended.

The untuned model, the anchor and the baselines.

Laya zero-shot is the untuned Laya model answering the same questions. The anchor is the December 2024 ModernBERT-large checkpoint (Warner et al., 2025), fine-tuned with the same heads and recipe as Laya-Fin; it was meant to show what training adds to a model whose pretraining ended before the sample. After one epoch its outputs are nearly constant, so we report it as uninformative, not as a null, and make no claim about the effect of training. The clean baselines are a ridge regression (Hoerl and Kennard, 1970) on sentence embeddings of the news, a gradient-boosted model (Ke et al., 2017) on price, volume and size alone, and a generative LLM prompted for the same nine-level forecast on a 2,000-event subsample. A pre-registered rule chose the LLM among models whose stated knowledge cutoff (April 2024) precedes the sample, so unlike the decision models it cannot have seen the sample in training. Two more baselines, vendor sentiment and a gradient-boosted model on the vendor’s topic tags, are built on labels the vendor produced after the fact; they are an upper bound that may carry look-ahead, not a benchmark.

3.4 Pre-registration, freeze and blinding

The pre-registration was written on 2026-10-24, before any panel, target or model output existed, and fixes the universe, the splits, the targets, the masking, the questions, every selection rule, the hypotheses with their families and corrections, the strategies and the inference. Three amendments were added the same day, also before any panel, target or model output existed: convergence to the news-implied value, a wider question battery and the firm-level explanation analysis. Later changes went only into an append-only, dated deviations log. On 2026-10-28, before any 2026 model call, a SHA-256 hash over the pre-registration, every configuration file and the analysis code was recorded and tagged in version control. The lock on the 2026 prices checks that hash. After the freeze it was opened to build the post-reaction states (reactions only) and then to release the test outcomes to the frozen analyses, the hypothesis tests first and the strategies later the same day; every read is logged.

3.5 Inference

The main statistic is the daily information coefficient,

ICt​(N^,z)=ρS​({N^i,t}i∈ℰt,{zi,t}i∈ℰt),IC¯=1T​∑t=1TICt​(N^,z),\mathrm{IC}_{t}(\hat{N},z)=\rho_{S}\bigl(\{\hat{N}_{i,t}\}_{i\in\mathcal{E}_{t}},\,\{z_{i,t}\}_{i\in\mathcal{E}_{t}}\bigr),\qquad\overline{\mathrm{IC}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathrm{IC}_{t}(\hat{N},z), (2)

the Spearman rank correlation ρS\rho_{S} between the readings and the moves across the events ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t} of session tt (sessions with at least five events), averaged over the TT sessions of a period. Its tt-statistic uses Newey–West standard errors with five lags (Newey and West, 1987). A positive IC means that the readings rank the day’s moves in the right order on average; the IC is the usual measure of a cross-sectional signal. The hypotheses that news is priced at the open compare the IC with the overnight move and with the move after the open:

H1: Δ=1T∑t[ICt(N^,zo​n)−ICt(N^,zi​d)]>0,H1b: 1T∑tICt(N^,zi​d)>0.\text{H1: }\Delta=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}\Bigl[\mathrm{IC}_{t}(\hat{N},z^{on})-\mathrm{IC}_{t}(\hat{N},z^{id})\Bigr]>0,\qquad\text{H1b: }\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}\mathrm{IC}_{t}(\hat{N},z^{id})>0. (3)

H1 says that the news is priced mostly at the open, H1b that it is not fully priced there, so that a position taken at the open can still earn. Both are tested one-sided with a stationary block bootstrap over sessions (Politis and Romano, 1994), with blocks of five sessions and 10,000 draws. H1b was added to the pre-registration before the freeze, because the pre-registered strategy that enters at the open needs it.

The five primary hypotheses (H1, H1b, H2, H3 and H4, defined where they are tested) form one family, corrected by Holm’s method at 0.05 (Holm, 1979); the secondary hypotheses form families corrected by Benjamini–Hochberg at q=0.10q=0.10 (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995). Regressions are pooled OLS with day-by-tier fixed effects and standard errors clustered by date and by firm (Cameron et al., 2011), with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors (Driscoll and Kraay, 1998) as a check. A primary result counts as a general claim only if it holds with the same sign and p<0.05p<0.05 for the primary instrument and for the anchor; if it holds for the primary instrument alone, it is model-specific. Because the anchor is uninformative and the commercial models failed the screens, no result in this paper can be more than model-specific: every result below is a statement about the models we tested, and we do not repeat the qualifier.

4 Clean validation did not survive the blinded test

Figure  compares each model’s daily IC with the close-to-close move on val-B, the quarter used for the final selection, with its IC on the test period. Laya-Fin was selected as the primary instrument because its val-B IC, 0.065 (t=3.64t=3.64), was the highest among the candidates eligible for that role; on val-A, which it was not trained on, its IC had been 0.055. On the test it fell to 0.020 (t=1.67t=1.67), below the lower end of its val-B 95% interval (0.030). The fall is not specific to the fine-tuned model. Every model whose val-B IC was clearly positive fell: the commercial models’ ICs roughly halved (d1-ultra’s from 0.097 to 0.039), and the generative LLM’s fell from 0.052 to 0.001 on its subsample. The clean price-only and embedding benchmarks are near zero in both periods. The highest test ICs belong to the two baselines built on vendor labels (0.055 for the tag model); because the vendor produced those labels after the fact, we read them as an upper bound that may contain look-ahead, not as a benchmark. Appendix Table  lists every model. A validation that looked clean on two quarters was weak evidence of what the model would do next; an exploratory split (Section ) locates the decline away from earnings days.

Table  reports the five primary hypotheses. None is supported for Laya-Fin (Holm-adjusted pp from 0.269 to 0.853). H1 and H1b, whether the news is priced at the open, are the subject of Section  and Table , and H2, the over/under regression, of Section  and Table . H3 asks whether the post-reaction judgment JJ adds to price-only and news-only features in predicting y2y_{2}, the move from the next open to the close of t+5t+5; the gain in IC is 0.0038 (p=0.054p=0.054). H4 asks whether the readings of materiality, surprise and expected magnitude predict the size of the day’s move, |zc​c||z_{cc}|, beyond a heterogeneous autoregressive model of realized volatility (Corsi, 2009), an earnings-day flag and the size tier; they add 0.0012 to the out-of-sample R2R^{2} (p=0.216p=0.216). Laya-Fin’s magnitude head ranks the size of the move (an AUC of 0.60 for moves of at least one typical day), so the models know which stocks will move a lot, but no better than the stocks’ own recent volatility.

5 Pre-open news is priced at the open

Equation () splits each day’s move at the open. Figure  and Table  show on which side of the open the models’ readings predict it. For the three commercial models the answer is clear. Their daily IC with the overnight move zo​nz_{on} is 0.074 to 0.077 (tt from 4.49 to 5.34), and their IC with the move after the open, zi​dz_{id}, is about zero (−-0.001 to 0.002). H1, the difference, is 0.075 for d1-ultra (95% interval 0.040 to 0.109, p=0.0001p=0.0001) and about the same for the other two. Sorted by d1-ultra’s reading, the top quintile of a day’s events moves 0.81 typical daily moves more overnight than the bottom quintile (t=5.6t=5.6). The untuned Laya model, which barely recognizes masked companies (Section ), shows the same pattern at a smaller scale (H1 =0.054=0.054, p=0.001p=0.001).

No model predicts the move after the open. H1b, the IC with zi​dz_{id}, is not significant for any model on the test: 0.010 for Laya-Fin (t=0.8t=0.8), and between −-0.017 and 0.002 for the others. This matters for Laya-Fin, whose validation signal seemed to reach past the open: on val-B its IC with zi​dz_{id} was 0.054 (t=2.89t=2.89), as large as its IC with zo​nz_{on}. That is why H1b was added to the pre-registration before the freeze. On the test, both of Laya-Fin’s ICs are small, and neither hypothesis is supported.

What the overnight IC measures.

The overnight move includes trading after the previous close and before the open, and pre-market trading starts at 04:00 ET. Part of zo​nz_{on} has therefore already happened when the model reads the news at 09:15, so the overnight IC partly measures how well a reading lines up with a move the market is already making, not only a forecast of the move between 09:15 and the open. The pre-registered analysis scores the readings against the whole overnight move and does not split it at 09:15. Either way, the part of the news that the readings capture is in the price by the open, and nothing measurable is left for a trader who enters there.

Robustness.

No pre-registered robustness variant changes these conclusions (Appendix Figure ): dollar-volume tiers, dropping articles with date-only or hour-rounded time stamps, a non-overlapping sample, placebo-adjusted targets, a 60-session volatility, dropping delisting horizons and dropping text about price moves. Unmasking does not raise d1-ultra’s IC: on 5,923 test events its IC with zc​cz_{cc} is 0.026 with masked states and 0.029 with the same states unmasked. The timing of the news matters. d1-ultra’s overnight IC is 0.115 (t=5.0t=5.0) when the latest article arrives between 08:00 and 09:15, 0.061 when it arrives between 04:00 and 08:00, and not significant when it precedes 04:00 (0.024). The closer to the open the news arrives, the more of the overnight move the reading lines up with.

6 The models cannot tell over- from under-reaction

6.1 The over/under regression

The central pre-registered hypothesis, H2, asks whether a model’s reading of the news separates the part of a day’s move that will persist from the part that will reverse. After the close (D2) we regress the next week’s move on the news-implied move and on the day’s move:

yi,t=a+b​N^i,t+c​Gi,t+αd⁡(t)×τ⁡(i)+εi,t,y_{i,t}=a+b\,\hat{N}_{i,t}+c\,G_{i,t}+\alpha_{d(t)\times\tau(i)}+\varepsilon_{i,t}, (4)

where yi,t=y2y_{i,t}=y_{2} is the abnormal move from the next open to the close of t+5t+5 in typical-move units, N^i,t\hat{N}_{i,t} is the model’s reading of the day’s news (all of it, up to the close, with price language removed), Gi,t=zi,tc​cG_{i,t}=z^{cc}_{i,t} is the day’s move and αd⁡(t)×τ⁡(i)\alpha_{d(t)\times\tau(i)} is a day-by-tier fixed effect; there is no conditioning on the size of GG. H2 predicts b>0b>0 (moves the news explains persist: underreaction to news) and c<0c<0 (moves the news does not explain reverse: overreaction to price); both must hold, and each is tested one-sided with standard errors clustered by date and firm.

Table  reports the estimates. For Laya-Fin, b=−0.044b=-0.044 (p=0.62p=0.62) and c=−0.015c=-0.015 (p=0.11p=0.11) on 17,188 events. The reversal coefficient has the predicted sign for every model but is never significant, and the news coefficient is not positive: d1-ultra’s is −-0.076 (p=0.99p=0.99 for a positive effect). The two earlier decision points, reported outside the family, do not change the picture. None of the eight pre-registered heterogeneity cuts (the three size tiers, quantified against story news, small moves, press wires, low usual coverage and busy days) changes Laya-Fin’s coefficients (Benjamini–Hochberg q≥0.74q\geq 0.74; Appendix Table ), and neither does the style of the coverage: a more promotional or sensational tone, a dimension of text separate from its content (Wegmann et al., 2026), does not predict reversal (H6; Appendix Table ).

6.2 Convergence to the news-implied value

The convergence analysis asks the same question along the whole path from the open to t+20t+20. For each rung hh of a ladder from the open to the close of t+20t+20, we regress the level move from the previous close to hh on the news-implied value:

CARi,hlvl=κhVi+αd⁡(t)×τ⁡(i)+εi,h,h∈{Ot,10:00,Ct,Ct+1,Ct+2,Ct+5,Ct+10,Ct+20},\mathrm{CAR}^{\mathrm{lvl}}_{i,h}=\kappa_{h}V_{i}+\alpha_{d(t)\times\tau(i)}+\varepsilon_{i,h},\qquad h\in\{O_{t},\ \text{10:00},\ C_{t},\ C_{t+1},\ C_{t+2},\ C_{t+5},\ C_{t+10},\ C_{t+20}\}, (5)

where CARi,hlvl\mathrm{CAR}^{\mathrm{lvl}}_{i,h} is the cumulative abnormal return in typical daily moves, without square-root-of-time scaling, so that it is comparable with VV. κh=1\kappa_{h}=1 means that by rung hh the price has moved all the way to the model’s value; a rising κh\kappa_{h} means drift toward it and a falling one means reversal.

Prices move part of the way to the model’s value on day tt and no further (Figure ; Appendix Table ). For Laya-Fin, κh\kappa_{h} is 0.36 at the close and 0.26 at t+20t+20; for d1-ultra the path is higher and has the same shape, from 0.59 at the close to 0.36 at t+20t+20. Neither pre-registered increase from the open to t+20t+20 is significant (p=0.47p=0.47 for Laya-Fin and 0.83 for d1-ultra). Prices also drift in VV’s direction before the event: five sessions earlier, d1-ultra’s top decile stood −-1.19 and its bottom decile 1.54 relative to the previous close. The states describe the company’s recent abnormal performance in words, so part of VV reflects momentum.

Because VV is a model’s estimate, a slope below one does not by itself mean that the market underreacts. Under classical measurement error, the level of κh\kappa_{h} mixes market efficiency with model noise, while the shape of the ladder (a rise or a fall after the decision point) is identified up to a positive factor (Appendix ). The informative fact is therefore the fade after the close: the part of the day’s move that lines up with the news does not continue, and partly gives back, although the pre-registered increase is not significant, so the fade is descriptive. The gap between the model’s value and the price does not close either: its half-life is not reached within 20 trading days for any model, and because VV is small next to the day’s move, the pre-registered gap-closure test measures how much of the day’s move reverses, not convergence to VV (Appendix ).

6.3 Under, over and the size of the move

The post-reaction reading classifies each event as an underreaction, a fair reaction or an overreaction, by how far the day’s move fell short of or exceeded the model’s value. Figure  (a) follows d1-ultra’s classes after the close, signed in the direction of the news. The 5,021 “Under” events moved against the news on day tt and never catch up (−-1.04 typical moves at t+20t+20, against a mean value of 0.38); the “Over” events give back part of their move, from 3.16 at the close to 2.82. Laya-Fin calls too few events either way to draw. Panel (b) asks the question by the size of the move instead: moves of at least three typical days reverse slightly in every tercile of news strength (two of the three intervals include zero), and smaller moves show small means of both signs. There is no sign that important news with a small move is underpriced.

Two descriptive cuts, pre-registered for reporting but not as tests, show where convergence is strongest. Laya-Fin’s slope at the close is 0.75 for the 100 largest companies against 0.23 and 0.25 for the other tiers. And by d1-ultra’s own label of the news, prices at t+20t+20 reflect the value of numerical news (κt+20=0.78\kappa_{t+20}=0.78, p=0.002p=0.002) but not that of narrative news (−-0.04), a pattern that echoes the earlier finding that markets treat numbers and stories differently (Kargarzadeh et al., 2026).

7 News explains little of a stock’s own move; the commercial models are overconfident

7.1 Explaining realized moves

Roll (1988) asked how much of a stock’s daily return public news explains, and Kelly et al. (2026) revisit the question for the market with generative AI. We ask it for single stocks, out of sample. For every covered company-day of the test period (days without selected news enter with zero news features, as in Roll), we build up the explanation of the stock-specific move zc​cz_{cc} step by step: the market and the sector (Roll’s first step), then the pre-open news reading, then the reading of all the day’s news, and finally the post-reaction reading’s explanation of the move, which reads the realized move and is therefore an attribution, not a forecast. Each step is a ridge regression fitted on validation data by the pre-registered protocol and scored on the test by

ROOS2=1−∑i,t(yi,t−y^i,t)2∑i,t(yi,t−y¯ref)2,Δ​Rs2=ROOS2​(s)−ROOS2​(s−1),R^{2}_{\mathrm{OOS}}=1-\frac{\sum_{i,t}\bigl(y_{i,t}-\hat{y}_{i,t}\bigr)^{2}}{\sum_{i,t}\bigl(y_{i,t}-\bar{y}_{\mathrm{ref}}\bigr)^{2}},\qquad\Delta R^{2}_{s}=R^{2}_{\mathrm{OOS}}(s)-R^{2}_{\mathrm{OOS}}(s-1), (6)

where y¯ref\bar{y}_{\mathrm{ref}} is the reference the frozen specification fixes (a zero forecast for the stock-specific move, and the val-B mean for the size of the move in H4), ROOS2​(s)R^{2}_{\mathrm{OOS}}(s) is the fit of steps one to ss, and Δ​Rs2\Delta R^{2}_{s} is what step ss adds to the steps before it. A positive ROOS2R^{2}_{\mathrm{OOS}} means the step predicts better than the reference on data it was not fitted on.

The news explains little of a stock’s own move (Figure , Table ). The market and the sector explain 25.3% of the total daily variance. Of the stock-specific part, the reading of all the day’s news explains 0.25% for Laya-Fin and 0.82% for d1-ultra, much of it already knowable before the open. H5, the secondary hypothesis that this step is positive, is supported for both models (Benjamini–Hochberg q=0.058q=0.058 for Laya-Fin). Reading the realized move explains far more: d1-ultra’s explanation step reaches 15.8% of the stock-specific variance on all covered days and 37.5% on days with news. Yet being explained does not predict persistence. In the pre-registered persistence regression the coefficient on the explanation is −-0.062 after the close (p=0.95p=0.95 for a positive effect): explained moves do not persist more than unexplained ones, and if anything reverse slightly more.

7.2 Calibration

The pre-registered calibration metric is the expected calibration error (Pakdaman Naeini et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2017): the pre-open reading’s nine levels are grouped into three classes (a fall, no move and a rise, split at half a typical daily move), and the top class’s stated probability is compared with its hit rate against the realized five-day move, in 15 equal-width bins. Laya-Fin’s error is small (0.057) only because its probabilities barely leave the validation base rates: its log-loss improves on them by 0.001. The commercial models are overconfident. Their stated probabilities overstate their hit rates, with errors from 0.209 to 0.361 and negative log-loss skill, and a single temperature fitted on val-A lowers d1-ultra’s error from 0.260 to 0.155 (Appendix Table  and Figure ). Calibration does not come with the decision-model interface; it has to be checked.

8 What the models know about masked firms

Masking removes names, but news is distinctive: a drug approval, a store count or a guidance range can point to one company. We measure how often a model recognizes the company behind a masked state. Each of 400 masked val-A states is shown with four candidate companies from the same sector and size tier, the true one and three distractors chosen to match its news activity, and the model picks one. For model mm,

Accm=1n∑i=1n𝟏[c^i=ci],excessm=Accm−p0,\mathrm{Acc}_{m}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\bigl[\hat{c}_{i}=c_{i}\bigr],\qquad\text{excess}_{m}=\mathrm{Acc}_{m}-p_{0}, (7)

where cic_{i} is the true company, c^i\hat{c}_{i} the model’s choice and p0=0.28p_{0}=0.28 the matched baseline: the accuracy of a guess that uses no reading, only the candidates’ news activity. Intervals are Wilson score intervals (Wilson, 1927). The matched baseline matters: with distractors drawn at random, a guess based on news activity alone already scores 36%, because the true company always has news.

The commercial decision models recognize the company far more often than the baseline (Figure ): from 62% of states (mercury-decide) to 74% (d1-ultra), and 66% and 68% for the other two comparators. The open-weights Laya model, the base of Laya-Fin, does so in 32%, close to the baseline. All of the commercial models therefore fail the pre-registered screen of 40%, and every model in the figure was released after the sample ended: Laya on 2026-09-18 and the commercial models between 2026-10-12 and 2026-10-16. Their training data are undisclosed, so we cannot rule out that they saw text from the test period.

Recognition is not the same as remembering returns, and three results suggest that it did not drive the commercial models’ overnight signal. The open-weights Laya model, which recognizes masked companies barely more often than the baseline, shows the same split between the overnight move and the move after the open (Section ); unmasking the states does not raise d1-ultra’s IC; and the commercial models’ ICs fell from validation to test as the other signals’ did, which is not what an advantage from having seen the test period would produce. None of the three is a test of memorization. The result is, however, a warning for backtests of language models on historical news: masking hides names, not companies. The pre-registered forward test (Section ) asks the question directly, on news published after the models were released.

9 Economic significance

The pre-registered strategies turn each reading into a daily long-short book within size tiers, hedged against the market with SPY. The convergence strategy (S-CONV) buys the events whose price lies furthest below the model’s value (the top 20% of the gap UU between the value and the move so far) and sells those furthest above it, after the first half hour (D1) or after the close (D2). Three more families rank the pre-open reading, entering at the open (S-D0), and the post-reaction judgment JJ, signed by the move, at 10:00 (S-D1) and after the close (S-D2). An RG book trades only the events the model calls an under- or over-reaction, and a gated book only its most confident readings. Costs are charged at 5, 10 and 20 basis points per side on both legs and on the hedge. Each book is compared with 100 books built on random signals over the same events, and its Sharpe ratio is deflated (Bailey and López de Prado, 2014) for the 545 trials the ledger held when the strategies were evaluated: every selection of filters, encodings, models and baselines, and every strategy variant up to then (Appendix ).

No pre-registered strategy is worth trading after costs (Table  and Figure ). Gross of costs, no book reaches the 95th percentile of its random-signal placebo, and Laya-Fin’s post-reaction book after the close falls below the 5th (percentile 3), as expected of judgments that carry no positive information about the next week. Net of 10 basis points every main book loses except the tiny RG book, which holds one stock a side on a handful of days. The convergence strategy is, in effect, a price-only gap fade: because the model’s value is small next to the day’s move, ranking by the gap buys the day’s losers and sells its winners. The two books share 92% of their positions, and their daily returns correlate 0.96. The highest gross Sharpe ratio, 1.88 for the pre-open book restricted to Laya-Fin’s most confident readings and held to the next close, breaks even at 8.3 basis points per side, and the one-day books turn over about 4.4 times their capital a day, so costs decide their sign. The largest deflated-Sharpe probability of any test book is 0.024. Short-sale borrow costs, which would lower every net figure, are not modeled.

10 Exploratory analyses (post hoc): where the signal lives

Everything in this section is exploratory. The analyses were requested after unblinding, they are outside every pre-registered family and they support no claim; they suggest where to look, and the forward test of Section  re-tests two of them as pre-registered hypotheses. Before this study was designed, the authors’ AI research assistant had looked at two of the statistics below on the test period (hit rates and mean moves by conviction band, and the statistics of the 10:00 reading), and those looks shaped it. Every exploratory variant is logged as a trial: the ledger grew from 545 to 1,620 trials.

Earnings days carry the signal.

In a post hoc split, every signal’s pre-open IC is concentrated on the 1,128 test events with a scheduled earnings report, and there it held in all three periods. Laya-Fin’s IC with zc​cz_{cc} on earnings days was 0.125, 0.106 and 0.134 on val-A, val-B and the test, against 0.013 on the other test events; d1-ultra’s was 0.223 on the test (t=8.1t=8.1). The fall from validation to test of Section  is therefore a fall on the other events. Even on earnings days the signal is priced at the open: d1-ultra’s earnings-day IC on the test is 0.238 with zo​nz_{on} and 0.034 with zi​dz_{id}.

Selective prediction: the overnight signal concentrates in the most confident calls.

We ranked events post hoc by conviction, the size of |N^||\hat{N}| against its val-A distribution, and kept only the top share of them, which traces a coverage curve (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017) (Figure ). d1-ultra’s mean overnight move in the direction of its reading, sign⁡(N^)⋅zo​n\mathrm{sign}(\hat{N})\cdot z_{on}, is 0.93 typical moves in its top 10% on the test, against 0.21 for all events, and the pattern held in both validation quarters. After the open, selectivity gains little: no test interval of the top share’s mean move after the open excludes zero at any coverage.

Watching the open adds nothing.

In a post hoc comparison, the reading at 10:00, after the first half-hour bar, never predicts the rest of the day better than the pre-open reading on val-B or the test, and the revision from the pre-open to the 10:00 reading has a zero or negative IC with the move from 10:00 to the close (Laya-Fin −-0.036 on the test, t=−2.3t=-2.3). The models seem to over-update toward the first bar, but the comparison involves many statistics, so this exploratory pattern is weak evidence.

Validation-to-test decay, the strongest instance.

A post hoc conditioning study asked whether the after-the-open signal sign⁡(N^)⋅zi​d\mathrm{sign}(\hat{N})\cdot z_{id} is stronger under some condition (the type and timing of the news, the day, the stock, the models’ internals, agreement between models and a cost hurdle) for 75 (model, condition) pairs. A strict rule, fixed before its test run, selected the pairs positive with t≥1t\geq 1 in both validation quarters and a pooled t≥2t\geq 2, and 8 passed. On the test, 5 of them changed sign and the other 3 are small (Appendix Figure ). Their tradable versions had in-sample gross Sharpe ratios up to 6.8 on val-B; on the test, none reaches the 90th percentile of its placebo, and every one loses net of 10 basis points.

11 Limitations and the forward test

Limitations.

The sample is the S&P 500, the largest and most closely followed US stocks; smaller stocks, where news may diffuse more slowly (Hong et al., 2000), may behave differently. The horizon is daily, with one intraday decision point at 10:00 built from 30-minute bars whose first bar starts at the first trade, not at the opening auction. The analysis scores the pre-open readings against the whole overnight move and does not split it at the 09:15 reading, so it cannot say how much of that move happened before the reading. The test period is seven months long (140 sessions with D0 events), so small ICs are hard to detect, and the selection rested on two validation quarters of 59 sessions each. The trained instruments were trained once, with one seed and one epoch; the anchor learned the size of moves but not their direction and is uninformative, so the study says nothing about what fine-tuning adds. The commercial models failed the pre-registered screens and were released after the sample, so contamination cannot be ruled out. Five of the authors wrote the earlier study (Kargarzadeh et al., 2026), whose 2023–2026 sample overlaps our test period; none of its statistics is a test in this paper, but its authors had seen aggregate news reactions that include early 2026 before this design was fixed. The vendor-label baselines rest on labels produced after the fact. Masking leaves small residues of names and dates, below half a percent of states. The strategies charge flat costs per side and model no borrow costs or market impact, and the hedge removes market risk only. Some pre-registered items were not run or not completed: three robustness variants that needed new model calls (a summary-text variant, vendor tags in the text and a 09:30 news cutoff; the 08:00 cutoff is approximated), the second and third training seeds, and 210 rate-limited requests of the ablations, which were not retried.

The forward test.

The cleanest test of memorization uses news published after every model’s release. Seven hypotheses for such a test were pre-registered on 2026-10-29, before any news from the forward window was exported and before any forward-period model call; the window runs from the first session after 2026-10-21 for at least three months, including the January–February 2027 earnings season, with the frozen pipeline run unchanged. They are:

  • •

    F1, memorization: for each commercial model, the change in IC from the test to the forward window minus the same change for the clean baselines is negative (Holm across the three models);

  • •

    F2, entity against event knowledge: company identification on masked forward states against masked test states, and against the matched baseline;

  • •

    F3, the conviction book: the pre-open book restricted to each model’s top tenth of |N^||\hat{N}| (thresholds fixed from val-A) has a positive net Sharpe ratio;

  • •

    F4, priced at the open: the frozen H1 and H1b on the forward window;

  • •

    F5, over-updating: the IC of the revision after the first half hour with the rest of the day’s move (two-sided);

  • •

    F6, overconfidence: the commercial models’ expected calibration error exceeds Laya-Fin’s (Holm across the three models);

  • •

    F7, conviction concentration: the mean signed overnight move of the top tenth by conviction exceeds that of all events (Holm across four models).

F5 and F7 turn exploratory results of Section , and F6 a descriptive comparison of Section , into confirmatory tests. The forward test has not been run. The robustness runs of the anchor (seeds 17 and 23 and a longer training run), fixed before unblinding, have not been run either; they are robustness only and cannot change any verdict here.

12 Conclusion

AI decision models read financial news well enough to line up with how a stock opens, and not well enough to forecast what it does after that. A fine-tuned open-weights model that looked convincing on two validation quarters did not survive a blinded test. The commercial models kept a signal, but only in the overnight gap, where the market had already priced the news before anyone could trade on it at the open, as an efficient market would (Fama, 1970). The models could not tell an overreaction from an underreaction, their calls of underreaction never caught up, and no pre-registered strategy survived costs and selection. Out of sample, news explains a fraction of a percent of a stock’s own daily variance, and the commercial models’ stated probabilities overstate their accuracy.

Three recommendations follow for anyone who backtests language-model readings of news. First, split the return at the open: a pre-open signal can be traded only if it predicts the move after the open, and a close-to-close backtest credits it with a move nobody could trade. Second, measure recognition, not just masking: report how often the model names the masked company against a matched baseline, and where possible test on news published after the model’s release, as our pre-registered forward test will. Third, freeze and count, as OLIVIA prescribes (Table ): select on validation data only, freeze the plan by hash, and log every trial and deflate for them; the strongest exploratory pattern we found, with in-sample Sharpe ratios up to 6.8, reversed on the test. The market reads the news first.

Appendix A Pre-registration and deviations

The pre-registration fixes every definition, constant, split, hypothesis and selection rule. After it was written, changes could only be appended to its deviations log, each with its date, the section it touches, the reason and whether it came before or after the freeze; the freeze record holds the log’s length at the freeze, and the lock refused to release the test outcomes unless the log was an unchanged prefix of the current one. The full log is in the replication package. Most entries make precise what the pre-registration left open (how a filter reaches its budget, which events a sample holds, how a variable is scaled) and were written before the freeze. The material deviations are these.

  • •

    Amendments before any data. Convergence to the news-implied value, a wider question battery and the firm-level explanation analysis were added on the day the pre-registration was written.

  • •

    Masking. The masking rules were widened several times before the freeze, after independent checks found residual names, dates and price moves; non-English articles, move explainers and running market stories were excluded; residues below half a percent of states were accepted and disclosed.

  • •

    The commercial models failed the pre-registered screens. Instead of dropping them, the three with the highest second-stage IC were kept as screen-failing, model-specific comparators (before the freeze).

  • •

    Training. The trained instruments are one seed and one epoch each, not the pre-registered three-seed ensemble, because of the compute available; the other seeds are robustness runs, fixed before unblinding and not yet run.

  • •

    H1b (the IC with the move after the open) was added to the primary family before the freeze, because the strategy that enters at the open needs it.

  • •

    Company identification was re-run with activity-matched distractors before the freeze, because a guess from news activity alone beat chance in the original design.

  • •

    Items not run. Three robustness variants needed new model calls and were not run (a summary-text variant, vendor tags in the text and a 09:30 news cutoff); the 08:00 cutoff is approximated from time stamps. Of the ablation requests, 210 were rate-limited and not retried.

  • •

    The canary. After the freeze, a stability check that repeats earlier requests fired for span-02 before production. Its build string was unchanged and the drift was close to its own repeat noise, so production went ahead under a rule recorded before the end-of-production check: a model counts as updated only if its build changes or two independent checks fire. At the end of production neither condition held for any model. The figures and tables mark span-02 with ‡ for this reason.

  • •

    The price-only baseline’s post-close predictions were moved after unblinding, because one of their inputs, the day’s overnight move, is a test-period outcome; the model was unchanged and first reproduced its validation predictions exactly.

  • •

    Analysis and strategies. The operationalization of the frozen specification and of the strategies was written before the outcomes were read; three code fixes found when the code first met the test data changed no pre-registered number.

  • •

    Exploratory work after unblinding is dated in the log. The conditioning study’s validation selection was committed before its single test run; its two definitional choices (the VIX close of the previous session, read from a registered copy of the market data, and payroll release dates added from the Bureau of Labor Statistics) were made on validation data.

  • •

    The forward test was pre-registered after the paper’s analyses, before any forward-period news was exported and before any forward-period model call (Section ).

Appendix B Notation

Appendix C The deflated Sharpe ratio

For a book with TT daily net returns, a per-period Sharpe ratio SR^\widehat{\mathrm{SR}}, skewness γ^3\hat{\gamma}_{3} and kurtosis γ^4\hat{\gamma}_{4}, the deflated-Sharpe probability (Bailey and López de Prado, 2014) is computed as

DSR=Φ⁡((SR^−SR0)​T−11−γ^3​SR^+γ^4−14​SR^2),SR0=𝒱​[(1−γ)​Φ−1​(1−1N)+γ​Φ−1​(1−1N​e)],\mathrm{DSR}=\Phi\!\left(\frac{(\widehat{\mathrm{SR}}-\mathrm{SR}_{0})\sqrt{T-1}}{\sqrt{1-\hat{\gamma}_{3}\,\widehat{\mathrm{SR}}+\tfrac{\hat{\gamma}_{4}-1}{4}\,\widehat{\mathrm{SR}}^{2}}}\right),\qquad\mathrm{SR}_{0}=\sqrt{\mathcal{V}}\left[(1-\gamma)\,\Phi^{-1}\!\left(1-\frac{1}{N}\right)+\gamma\,\Phi^{-1}\!\left(1-\frac{1}{N\mathrm{e}}\right)\right], (A1)

where Φ\Phi is the standard normal distribution function, γ\gamma the Euler–Mascheroni constant, NN the number of trials and 𝒱=(1+SR^2/2)/(T−1)\mathcal{V}=(1+\widehat{\mathrm{SR}}^{2}/2)/(T-1) the variance of a Sharpe-ratio estimate (Lo, 2002); the analytic variance is used because most of the ledger’s other trials are information coefficients, recalls and losses, not Sharpe ratios. SR0\mathrm{SR}_{0} is the Sharpe ratio that the best of NN independent trials without skill would reach in expectation, so it rises with NN: a book must beat it, not zero. With the 545 trials of the ledger when the pre-registered strategies were evaluated and 139 test days, SR0\mathrm{SR}_{0} is 0.26 per day for the convergence strategy, far above any book’s daily Sharpe ratio. The exploratory books of Section  were deflated with all 1,620 trials of the ledger after the exploratory study, which raises the bar further.

Appendix D Additional pre-registered results

This appendix gives the pre-registered results that the main text cites but does not show: every model’s IC and cost (Table ), the robustness variants (Figure ), the heterogeneity cuts (Table ), the secondary hypotheses (Table ), the convergence ladder with what it identifies and the gap-closure test (Appendix  and Table ), and calibration (Table  and Figure ). Further tables and figures are in the replication package.

D.1 The convergence ladder: what it identifies, and gap closure

What the ladder identifies.

A slope below one in Equation () does not by itself mean that the market underreacts, because VV is a model’s estimate. A standard errors-in-variables argument (Hausman, 2001) makes this precise; we add it as an interpretation, not as a new test. Suppose the model’s value is a noisy measure of the true news-implied value, V=V∗+eV=V^{*}+e, with classical error: ee has mean zero and is independent of V∗V^{*} and of the regression error, after the fixed effects are partialled out. Then the slope converges to

κ^h→θV​κh∗,θV=Var⁡(V∗)Var⁡(V∗)+Var⁡(e)≤1,\hat{\kappa}_{h}\;\to\;\theta_{V}\,\kappa^{*}_{h},\qquad\theta_{V}=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(V^{*})}{\operatorname{Var}(V^{*})+\operatorname{Var}(e)}\leq 1, (A2)

where κh∗\kappa^{*}_{h} is the slope on the true value. Two consequences follow. First, the level of κh\kappa_{h} mixes market efficiency with model noise, so κh<1\kappa_{h}<1 alone is not evidence of underreaction. Second, the shape of the ladder is identified up to the same factor: on a common set of events, κ^h′−κ^h→θV​(κh′∗−κh∗)\hat{\kappa}_{h^{\prime}}-\hat{\kappa}_{h}\to\theta_{V}(\kappa^{*}_{h^{\prime}}-\kappa^{*}_{h}). The factor is positive, so the sign is preserved: a rise after the decision point means drift toward the true value and a fall means reversal. This is why the pre-registered tests read the ladder’s shape (the increase κt+20−κOt\kappa_{t+20}-\kappa_{O_{t}} and the gap closure below) rather than its level. Table  gives every rung for every model.

Gap closure.

The gap between the model’s value and the price after the reaction, Ui,τ=Vi−Gi,τlvlU_{i,\tau}=V_{i}-G^{\mathrm{lvl}}_{i,\tau} at decision point τ\tau (D1 or D2), should close if the price converges to the value; GlvlG^{\mathrm{lvl}} is the observed reaction divided by σc​c\sigma^{cc} without a square-root-of-time factor, so that moves at different horizons add up. With AR⁡(τ→h)\mathrm{AR}(\tau\to h) the abnormal move from the decision point to rung hh,

ARi​(τ→h)σic​c=αd⁡(t)×τ⁡(i)+λh​Ui,τ+ψh​Vi+εi,h,h∗=min⁡{h:λh≥12},\frac{\mathrm{AR}_{i}(\tau\to h)}{\sigma^{cc}_{i}}=\alpha_{d(t)\times\tau(i)}+\lambda_{h}\,U_{i,\tau}+\psi_{h}V_{i}+\varepsilon_{i,h},\qquad h^{*}=\min\bigl\{h:\lambda_{h}\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\bigr\}, (A3)

where λh\lambda_{h} is the share of the gap closed by rung hh, ψh\psi_{h} captures convergence to a shrunken value, and the half-life h∗h^{*} is “not reached” when no rung qualifies. The gap does not close. After the close, Laya-Fin’s λh\lambda_{h} is −-0.007 at t+1t+1, 0.026 at t+5t+5 (p=0.16p=0.16) and 0.050 at t+20t+20; from 10:00 every λh\lambda_{h} is at or below zero; and the half-life is not reached within t+20t+20 for any model. The λh\lambda_{h} are almost the same for every model because VV is small next to the day’s move, so that U≈−GlvlU\approx-G^{\mathrm{lvl}}: λh\lambda_{h} measures how much of the day’s move reverses, not convergence to VV. The tracking error between the price and the model’s value is no smaller than that of a naive value of zero (ratio 1.001 at t+20t+20, p=0.87p=0.87). None of the convergence tests is supported after Benjamini–Hochberg (Table ).

Appendix F The replication package

The project’s repository, https://github.com/AmirDehkordi/NewsAction, is the replication package. It holds the pre-registration with its amendments and its full deviations log, the freeze record, the code of every stage with its tests, the committed outputs and a report of every stage, the ledgers of trials, spend and test-data access, and the sources of this paper, whose tables, figures and numbers one command rebuilds from the committed outputs without raw data, an API or a GPU (two strategy tables, which need position-level files kept with the data, are carried over as committed). The data are private and are not part of the package: the news text is licensed and is not redistributed, and neither are the price data or the index membership.
